title: Yudha Kāṇḍa: The Great War of Liberation
body:
Yudha Kāṇḍa: The Great War of Liberation

The Tidings Conveyed

The search party came before Rāma, and Hanumān came forward to deliver his news, and the moment of the delivering is one of the tenderest in the whole epic, for it ended the longest and deepest of Rāma’s griefs, and it did so through the simplest of gestures.

Hanumān did not begin with a long report. He knew what Rāma most needed to hear, and he said it first, in the fewest words, the words that would lift the whole weight of grief from his master’s heart in a single instant. Sītā has been found, he said. She is seen. She lives. Across the ocean, in Lankā, in the Ashokavana of Rāvaṇa, I have found her and seen her and spoken with her, and she lives, and she keeps faith, and she waits for you. And then, to prove it beyond any possibility of doubt, before Rāma could even fully absorb the words, Hanumān brought out the token, the Chūḍāmaṇi, Sītā’s own crest- jewel, and placed it in Rāma’s hands.

And Rāma took the jewel, and knew it, and the knowledge broke over him like a wave. Here was Sītā’s own ornament, the jewel from her own hair, that he knew, that no one could have counterfeited, the very thing she had worn; and it was warm, as it were, from her hand, carried across the ocean from the living captive to her grieving husband, the proof of everything: that she lived, that she was found, that she had kept faith, that she had sent this token of her love and her fidelity across all that distance to him. Rāma held the little jewel in his hands, and pressed it to his eyes, and to his heart, and wept, and his weeping now was not the weeping of the long grief that had nearly destroyed him but the weeping of a grief transformed at last into hope, of a longing that at last had an answer, of a love that had feared everything and now knew that the beloved lived and waited.

Let us feel the fullness of this moment, for the whole long agony of the story since the abduction has been building toward it. Since the empty cottage, since the wild grief in the forest, since the long search, Rāma has carried the terrible weight of not-knowing: whether Sītā lived, whether she suffered, whether she could ever be found, whether all his labour and longing were spent upon a captive already dead or lost beyond recovery. And now, in a single instant, through a few words and a small jewel, that whole weight was lifted. Sītā lived. Sītā was found. Sītā kept faith and waited. The not-knowing was over; the grief had an object and the object was recoverable; the long night of pure loss had ended in the certain dawn of hope. And the little jewel in his hands, warm with all it meant, was the sign and the seal of it, the touch of his living wife reaching him across the ocean, and Rāma wept over it with a joy that all his composure could not contain and that he did not try to contain, for this was joy that had earned its tears.

And when the first flood of it had passed, Rāma turned to Hanumān, and his gratitude to the faithful servant who had brought him this was beyond his power to express, and the tellers dwell on it, for the bond between Rāma and Hanumān is one of the most beautiful things in all the tale. Rāma embraced Hanumān, and he tried to thank him, and he found that he could not, that there was no reward, no gift, no honour equal to what Hanumān had done. What can I give you, he said in effect, that could ever match this service? You have crossed the impassable ocean; you have entered the enemy’s fortress; you have found my Sītā when I had begun to despair of finding her; you have comforted her and given her hope and brought me the certain knowledge that she lives; you have done what no other being in all the worlds could have done, and you have done it out of pure devotion, asking nothing. There is no reward that can equal such a deed. I have nothing to give you that is worthy of it. I can only give you my embrace, and my love, and my eternal gratitude, and the knowledge that as long as this story is told, your name will be joined to mine, and you will be honoured wherever I am honoured, for you have given me back my life. And Rāma embraced Hanumān as a brother, as a dearest friend, as one whose service had passed beyond the possibility of repayment into the realm of pure love, and the bond between them was sealed in that embrace, the bond of the perfect Lord and the perfect devotee, which is the very heart of what this story has to teach about love and service and devotion.

There is a deep truth in Rāma’s inability to reward Hanumān, and the tellers mean us to see it. For the highest service, the service given out of pure love, cannot be repaid, because it was never given for a reward; it stands outside the whole economy of giving and getting; it can only be met with love, with gratitude, with the recognition that here is something beyond price. Hanumān had not served Rāma for any reward; he had served out of pure devotion, for the joy of serving, for the love of the one he served; and such service can only be honoured, never repaid, for to repay it would be to reduce it to a transaction, and it was never a transaction but a gift of the whole self. Rāma understood this, and so he did not insult Hanumān’s devotion by offering a reward equal to it, for there was none; he offered instead the only fit response to such love, which is love, and gratitude, and the eternal bond of friendship. And in that response, the perfect devotion of Hanumān met the perfect love of Rāma, and the two were joined forever, and the tellers hold up their bond as the very model and ideal of what the love between the devotee and the divine can be.

So the tidings were conveyed, and Rāma’s long grief was ended, and his love and gratitude poured out upon the faithful Hanumān, and the whole weight of the story shifted now from sorrow toward action, from the finding of Sītā toward the winning of her. For now Rāma knew where she was, and knew she lived, and knew that the enemy’s city, for all its might, could be entered and burned; and there remained only to gather the army, and cross the ocean, and make war upon Lankā, and destroy Rāvaṇa, and take Sītā back with honour, exactly as she had said it must be done. The grief was over; the war was beginning; and the great host of the vānaras, with Rāma and Lakshmaṇa at its head and Hanumān and Sugrīva and all the mighty leaders of the monkey-people beside them, turned now toward the south, toward the sea, toward the golden city across the water, and the last and greatest movement of the story began.

The Army Moves Forward

With Sītā found and her captivity confirmed, there was no more reason for delay, and Rāma gave the word, and the great vānara host mobilized for war. Sugrīva summoned the full strength of his kingdom, the armies of the monkey- people gathered from every mountain and forest of the world, and they came, a multitude beyond counting, until the whole country seemed to move, and the army set out southward toward the sea, toward the crossing that would carry them to Lankā and to war.

The tellers give us the spectacle of that march, and it was a spectacle indeed. Imagine the vast host on the move: the earth trembling under the tread of numberless vānaras, the dust rising in a great cloud that darkened the sky, the din of the marching army rolling across the land like continuous thunder, the whole enormous force pouring southward with Rāma and Lakshmaṇa at its head, and Sugrīva the king, and Hanumān, and Angada, and Jāmbavān, and all the mighty leaders of the monkey-people, a river of warriors flowing toward the sea. It was an army such as the world had rarely seen, gathered for a righteous war, marching to break a fortress that had never been breached and to bring down a king who had never been conquered, and the sight and sound of it filled the lands it passed through with awe.

And Rāma led them, and the tellers pause on the change that had come over him, for the grieving husband of the forest was now a commander marching to war, and the two were held together in him. He had not ceased to be the man who wept over Sītā’s jewel; but that grief had been forged now into purpose, into the cold steady resolve of one who knows exactly what he must do and is going to do it. He led the host with the calm authority of a great captain, ordering the march, heartening the warriors, planning the campaign with Sugrīva and Lakshmaṇa and the vānara chiefs, and beneath all the calm command there burned the single unwavering purpose that had carried him from the empty cottage to this: to reach Sītā, to destroy the power that held her, to take her back with honour. The grief had become an army on the march, and the love had become a war.

They came at last to the shore of the southern sea, and there the great host halted, for before them lay the barrier that had stopped the searchers: the ocean, vast, deep, a hundred leagues of open water, and beyond it, invisible over the curve of the world, the golden city of Lankā. The army that had marched so mightily across the land now stood at the water’s edge and could go no further, for an army cannot leap as Hanumān had leapt; the whole host, for all its numbers and its strength, was stopped dead by the sea, exactly as the searchers had been stopped, and the same despair that had touched the search party now brushed the army, for how was such a host to cross such a sea?

The ocean lay before them, immense and impassable, a silent grey barrier between the army and its goal, and the whole enterprise, which had marched so confidently to the shore, now faced the question that the shore had always posed: how to cross. Hanumān alone had leapt it; but Hanumān was one, and here was a host of countless thousands, with no wings, no ships, no bridge, and a hundred leagues of open water between them and the enemy they had come so far to fight. The army made its camp along the shore, and Rāma and his captains looked out over the vast water toward the unseen city, and pondered the crossing, and the great question of how the ocean was to be passed hung over the whole host as it settled by the sea.

But the halting at the sea, though it posed a hard question, was also the completion of a great stage, and the tellers mark it as such. The alliance had been made; the search had succeeded; the army had been gathered and marched to the very edge of the enemy’s domain. Everything that could be done on the near side of the ocean had been done. What remained was the crossing, and then the war, and both of these were now close at hand, waiting only on the solving of the sea. And while Rāma’s host camped on the shore and pondered how to cross, on the far side of that same sea, in the golden city that had already once been entered and burned, a very different mood was gathering, for Lankā had seen a single servant of Rāma wreck its garden and slay its prince and burn its streets, and now word was coming that the master of that servant was marching to the sea with an army beyond counting, and the golden city that had never known fear was beginning, at last, to be afraid.

Anxiety in Lankā

Across the sea, in Lankā, the mood had changed, and this chapter belongs to that change, to the slow seeping of dread into a city that had never known it.

For Lankā had been, until now, a city wholly without fear. It was the seat of the mightiest power of the age; its king had conquered gods; its warriors were terrible; its walls had never been breached; and its people had lived in the settled arrogance of those who believe themselves untouchable, secure in the shadow of Rāvaṇa’s might, contemptuous of all the worlds they had subdued. Fear was a thing that happened to others, to the conquered, to the weak; it had no place in golden Lankā, the invincible fortress of the invincible king.

And then a single vānara had come, and the settled arrogance had cracked. Hanumān’s visitation had done more than wreck a garden and slay a prince and burn some streets; it had struck the first blow at the city’s deepest possession, its confidence, its sense of its own invulnerability. For if a single servant of the enemy could enter the impregnable city, wreck the royal pleasure-garden, slay a prince of the blood, defy the king in his own court, and burn the golden capital from end to end, and then leap away unharmed, then Lankā was not invulnerable after all; the walls could be passed; the fortress could be entered; the impossible could happen. The burning had left more than ashes; it had left doubt, the first doubt the proud city had ever known, and doubt, once admitted, spreads.

And now, on top of the doubt, came the news: that Rāma, the master of that single terrible servant, was marching to the sea with an army beyond counting, coming to make war on Lankā, coming for Sītā and for vengeance. And the doubt that Hanumān had planted began to grow, in the light of this news, into something closer to dread. For the reasoning was plain and cold, and it spread through the city in whispers: if one servant could do so much, what would the master do, and his whole host? The burning of Lankā by a single vānara had been a demonstration; the coming of Rāma’s army was the thing demonstrated; and the people of Lankā, looking at their fire-scarred city and hearing of the approaching host, began to feel, for the first time in their lives, the cold touch of fear.

And the tellers give us the omens, too, the physical signs of coming doom that began to trouble the city, for in the old understanding such great events cast their shadows before them, and the very elements gave warning of the ruin that approached. There were portents, dark and troubling: vultures and birds of ill omen gathering and circling over the city; strange tremors in the earth; unnatural changes in the light and the air; the sacred fires behaving ill; evil dreams troubling the sleep of the demons; all the signs by which, in the old belief, the cosmos itself announces an approaching catastrophe. These omens spread through Lankā, and deepened the dread, for they seemed to confirm what the news of Rāma’s army suggested, that the doom of the city was truly at hand, that the invincible fortress was facing, at last, its destruction.

And there were voices, too, the voices of the elder and wiser among the demons, the counsellors and ministers who had always known, or had come to see, that Rāvaṇa’s crime would bring ruin, and who now raised their warnings as the danger approached. For not all in Lankā were fools or fanatics; there were among the demons those with wisdom and foresight, who understood that the abduction of Sītā had been a catastrophic error, that it had brought upon the city an enemy it could not hope to defeat, that the whole disaster flowed from Rāvaṇa’s ungoverned lust and pride, and who now, in the growing dread, found the courage to say so, to warn the king, to counsel him even at this late hour to return Sītā and seek peace before the storm broke. Their warnings mostly went unheeded, for Rāvaṇa’s pride was not to be moved; but they were raised, and they added to the atmosphere of foreboding, the sense of a city divided between a proud king rushing toward ruin and the wiser souls who saw the ruin coming and could not turn him from it.

Let us mark the deep justice in this change of mood, for the tellers mean us to feel it. Lankā had made a whole world afraid; its king had terrorized the gods; its power had rested on the fear it inspired in others; and now, at last, fear had come home to Lankā itself. The city that had never feared was learning to fear; the fortress that had made others tremble was beginning to tremble; and the arrogance that had scorned all the worlds was cracking under the approach of a justice it could not escape. There is a rightness in it, a turning of the wheel, the terror-maker learning terror, the invincible learning its own vulnerability, the proud city beginning to pay, in dread, for all the dread it had inflicted. And the dread was just, for the doom was real; the omens did not lie; the wise counsellors were right; Rāma was coming, and Lankā would fall, and some in the city already knew it, and feared, and the fear was the first installment of the ruin.

So the mood in Lankā darkened toward dread, and the omens multiplied, and the wise warned and the proud refused to hear, and over the whole golden city there settled the heavy foreboding of a doom approaching across the sea. And in the midst of this gathering anxiety, Rāvaṇa, refusing still to feel the fear that had touched his people, refusing still to heed the omens or the warnings, called his council together, to plan not for peace but for war, to array the strength of Lankā against the coming enemy, and to hear from his commanders and his brothers the counsel that would either save the city or seal its doom.

Rāvaṇa Calls a Council Again

Rāvaṇa summoned his war council, the great lords and warriors and commanders of Lankā, and his brothers, to take counsel on the coming war, and the council reveals, in the sharp contrast between the voices raised in it, the whole moral division of Lankā, and the tragedy of a king who could hear only the counsel that flattered his folly.

The council assembled, and the greater part of it spoke as Rāvaṇa wished to hear. His generals and his champions, proud demon warriors confident in their own might, boasted of their strength and made light of the coming enemy. What is this Rāma, they said in effect, but a mere man, an exile, a wanderer of the forest, with an army of monkeys? What is such a foe to the might of Lankā, that has conquered gods and subdued the three worlds? Let him come; let him try his ocean; we will destroy him and his monkey-host and think nothing of it. There is no cause for concern, no need for peace or for the return of the woman; the whole matter is beneath our worry; we will crush this human and his beasts and add his defeat to the long roll of Lankā’s victories. So they boasted, one after another, the proud warriors of the demon race, flattering their king’s pride, making light of the danger, urging war and confidence and contempt for the enemy.

And there were among them those who boasted not merely from confidence but from the sycophant’s instinct to tell the king what he wished to hear, and these were the most dangerous of all, for they dressed their flattery as counsel and their cowardice-in-truth as courage-in-war. They saw that Rāvaṇa wished to keep Sītā and to fight, and so they told him that fighting was wise and keeping her was safe, not because they believed it, some of them, but because it was what the king wanted, and it is the way of a tyrant’s court that the truth is the one thing no one dares to speak.

But not all the voices were of this kind. For there were among the elder and wiser of the demons, and above all among Rāvaṇa’s own kin, those who saw the truth and had the courage, or the desperation, to speak it, and against the chorus of boasting there rose the heavy, solemn counsel of the wise, warning of the doom that the boasters would not see.

Consider first the matter of the enemy they made so light of, one wise voice urged. This Rāma you call a mere man, a mere exile, what has he already done? He destroyed Khara and Dūshaṇa and fourteen thousand of our warriors, alone, in a single battle. And his servant, a single vānara, entered our impregnable city, wrecked the royal garden, slew the prince Aksha, defied the king in his own court, and burned our golden capital to the ground, and leapt away unharmed. Is this the work of a mere man and a host of beasts to be despised? If one servant could burn Lankā, what will the master and his army do? You boast of our strength, but our strength has already been tested, in the person of that one vānara, and it was not enough even to hold him. Do not make light of this enemy; he is the mightiest we have ever faced; and we have brought him upon ourselves.

And the wisest went further, to the root of the matter, and counselled not merely caution in war but the undoing of the crime that had caused it. The truth, they said, is that this whole calamity springs from a single wrong: the taking of Sītā. She is another man’s wife, taken by force and deceit, and held against her will and against all dharma; and it is for her, and for the wrong of her taking, that this doom now approaches. There is one way, and only one, to avert it: return her. Give Sītā back to Rāma, with honour and with apology, and the cause of the war is removed, and the war itself may be averted, and Lankā may be saved. To keep her is to keep the crime, and to keep the crime is to keep the doom. Let the king put away his pride and his lust, and return the woman, and save his city and his people from the destruction that her keeping will surely bring. This is the counsel of wisdom: not war, but the undoing of the wrong that has made war inevitable.

So the council divided, and the division was the division of Lankā’s very soul: on one side the boasters and the flatterers, urging war and confidence and the keeping of Sītā; on the other the wise and the righteous, urging the return of the queen and the averting of the doom. And between them sat Rāvaṇa, who had the power to choose, and whose choice would decide the fate of his city and his race.

And here is the tragedy that the council exists to show us, and the tellers weight it heavily: that Rāvaṇa, given the truth plainly and the way of salvation clearly, chose to hear the flatterers and to ignore the wise. His pride could not bear the counsel that required him to admit his error, to give up his prize, to bow to the demands of dharma and return the woman he had stolen. It was easier, far easier, to hear the boasters who told him he was mighty and the enemy contemptible and the war certain to be won, than to hear the wise who told him he had done wrong and must undo it. And so, as tyrants do, as the proud do, as all of us are tempted to do, Rāvaṇa listened to the counsel that flattered his desire and ignored the counsel that challenged it, and inclined toward war, and toward the keeping of Sītā, and toward the doom that the wise had warned of and the flatterers had denied. There is a deep and universal lesson in this council, and it is one worth carrying away, for the failing it shows is not the demons’ alone. It is the failing of every proud heart that surrounds itself with those who echo its desires and shuts out those who speak the unwelcome truth; the failing of every power that mistakes flattery for loyalty and honest warning for disloyalty; the failing of every soul that, given the plain truth and the clear way of salvation, chooses instead the comfortable lie because the truth would cost its pride too much. Rāvaṇa’s ruin was not forced upon him; it was chosen, in this council, when he turned from the wise to the flatterers, from the truth to the comfortable lie, from the way of salvation to the way of doom. He was given every chance; the truth was spoken plainly in his own hall; and he refused it, because to accept it would have meant humbling his pride, and his pride was dearer to him than his city and his people and his own life. And so the council, which might have saved Lankā, instead sealed its doom, not because the truth was not spoken, but because the king would not hear it.

But there was one voice in that council not yet fully raised, one brother of Rāvaṇa whose righteousness ran deeper than the rest, who would not be content merely to counsel and be ignored, but would press the truth upon his brother to the very breaking point, and stake everything upon it, and, when the king refused, would make a choice that changed the whole course of the war. For Vibhīshaṇa, the righteous brother, was about to speak, and to keep speaking, and to force the issue to a crisis that would end in his exile from Lankā and his defection to Rāma.

Vibhīshaṇa

Vibhīshaṇa was Rāvaṇa’s brother, and he was a rākshasa by birth, but he was righteous by nature, and the story presents him as one of its great moral figures, a soul set in the very household of evil who yet held fast to dharma, and whose fidelity to the right, even against his own brother and his own kind, cost him his home and won him a place among the immortal exemplars of virtue.

He had counselled Rāvaṇa toward justice all along; he had opposed the abduction of Sītā from the first; he had urged again and again that she be returned and the crime undone. And now, in the council, with the war approaching and the doom gathering, Vibhīshaṇa made his stand, and he made it fully, holding nothing back, pressing the truth upon his brother with all the force of his conviction and all the love of a brother who would save his brother from ruin if he could.

Hear me, brother, Vibhīshaṇa urged, and hear me truly, for I speak not against you but for you, to save you and our house and our people from the destruction that is coming. This whole calamity has one cause, and one cause only: the taking of Sītā. You have done a grievous wrong. You have stolen another man’s wife, by force and by deceit, a woman of perfect virtue, and you hold her against her will and against all dharma, and it is for this wrong that Rāma comes, and it is this wrong that will destroy us all if it is not undone. There is no shame in undoing a wrong; the shame is in persisting in it. Return Sītā. Give her back to Rāma with honour and with apology; beg his forgiveness; and the cause of the war is removed, and Lankā is saved. I beg you, by our blood, by our house, by the love I bear you: put away your pride and your desire, and return this woman, and save us all. To keep her is to embrace our doom; to return her is to live. Choose life, brother. Choose the undoing of the wrong. Do not, for the sake of a lust that can never be satisfied and a pride that will not bend, drag our whole race down into the ruin that your crime has called upon us.

It was the counsel of pure wisdom and pure love, and it went to the very root of the matter, naming the wrong plainly and offering the one true way of salvation. And Rāvaṇa, hearing it, was enraged past all bearing.

For this was the one counsel Rāvaṇa could not endure to hear: the counsel that required him to admit his wrong, to give up his prize, to humble his pride, to bow to the demands of a dharma he had set himself above. That his own brother should say these things, should name his crime, should call his desire a lust and his firmness a folly, should urge him to surrender the woman and beg forgiveness of a human exile, was to Rāvaṇa an intolerable insult, a betrayal, an act of disloyalty in the very hour of danger. His fury blazed up, and he turned on his brother with rage and with contempt, and he heaped abuse upon him.

Traitor, he called him, and coward, and worse. You counsel surrender in the hour of war; you take the enemy’s part against your own blood; you would have me grovel before a human and give up what I have won, out of fear of his monkey-army. Is this the loyalty of a brother? You are no brother of mine; you are a coward and a turncoat, secretly on the enemy’s side, using the language of wisdom to cloak your treachery and your fear. Get out of my sight. I have no use for such counsel or for such a brother. And in his rage, the tellers say, Rāvaṇa spurned Vibhīshaṇa utterly, insulting him, rejecting him, and by some tellings kicking him or striking at him, driving his own righteous brother from the council and from the court in disgrace, casting him out for the crime of having spoken the truth.

And Vibhīshaṇa, so insulted, so rejected, so spurned for his wisdom and his love, faced now the hardest choice of his life, and how he made it is the moral heart of the chapter. He could have submitted, could have swallowed the insult and stayed, could have remained in Lankā out of loyalty to blood and country even as they rushed toward ruin, sharing their doom out of a misplaced fidelity. Many would have called that loyalty, and would have thought Vibhīshaṇa bound to stand with his brother and his people whatever they did, right or wrong.

But Vibhīshaṇa understood loyalty differently, and his understanding is the lesson of his story. He understood that true loyalty is not to blood or country regardless of right, but to dharma, to the truth, to the good; that to stand with one’s own kin in a manifest and ruinous wrong is not loyalty but complicity; and that a righteous soul, forced to choose between its people and the right, must choose the right, though it break every bond of blood and country and cost it everything. Rāvaṇa was in the wrong, catastrophically and unrepentantly; Lankā was rushing toward a doom it had earned; and to stay, to share their crime and their doom out of mere loyalty to blood, would have been to make himself a partner in the wrong. Vibhīshaṇa would not do it. If his brother would keep the stolen queen and rush toward ruin, Vibhīshaṇa would not go with him into that ruin; he would leave; he would go to Rāma, to the side of right, to the cause of dharma, though it meant abandoning his home, his brother, his people, and casting his lot with the enemy of his own kind. Let us weigh the enormity and the courage of this choice, for it is easy to state and terribly hard to make. Vibhīshaṇa was choosing to abandon his own brother, his own people, his own country, his whole world, and to go over to the side of those who were coming to destroy them, because he judged that his own side was in the wrong and the enemy in the right. There is no harder choice than this, to set the truth above one’s own blood, to stand against one’s own people when one’s own people are wrong, to bear the name of traitor for the sake of dharma; and the world is quick to call such a choice treachery, as Rāvaṇa called it. But the story is clear, and clears Vibhīshaṇa utterly: his choice was not treachery but the highest fidelity, fidelity to the right above all lesser loyalties, and it is held up as one of the noblest acts in the whole epic, the act of a soul that loved dharma more than it loved even its own kin, and that had the terrible courage to act on that love when the test came.

And so Vibhīshaṇa left Lankā. Spurned, insulted, rejected by his brother, he rose up and departed from the golden city and from all he had known, and with a few faithful companions he flew across the sea, across the very water that Rāma’s army stood halted before, to seek refuge with Rāma, to offer his allegiance to the cause of right, to stake his life on the side of dharma against his own blood and kind. He crossed the sea toward the enemy’s camp, an exile now himself, having chosen the truth over his home and his brother, and he came toward Rāma’s host not knowing how he would be received, whether as a welcome ally or as a suspected spy, staking everything on the hope that the champion of dharma would receive one who had given up everything for dharma’s sake.

The Vānaras’ Doubt

Vibhīshaṇa came across the sea and appeared above the vānara camp, seeking Rāma, and his coming threw the camp into a sharp debate, for here was a rākshasa, a demon, a brother of Rāvaṇa himself, coming from the enemy’s city to the very heart of Rāma’s host, and the question of whether to receive him or to destroy him was not a simple one, and the arguments on both sides reveal the differing wisdoms of Rāma’s counsellors.

For most of the vānara leaders, seeing a demon approach from Lankā, counselled suspicion and rejection. Sugrīva above all was wary, and his reasoning was the natural reasoning of caution in war. This is a demon, he warned, a rākshasa, and worse, the very brother of our enemy Rāvaṇa. Why should such a one come to us now, on the eve of battle, if not as a spy, a deceiver, an agent sent by Rāvaṇa to worm his way into our councils, to learn our plans, to betray us at the crucial hour? It is a trick, surely; it is too convenient; the enemy’s own brother does not simply defect to us out of love of righteousness on the very eve of war. Do not trust him. Do not receive him into our camp and our confidence. Send him away, or destroy him, but do not open our councils to one who is by blood and birth our enemy and who comes to us with a story too good to be true. So Sugrīva counselled, and many of the leaders agreed, and their caution was reasonable, for in war a defector from the enemy’s own royal house, arriving just before battle, is exactly what a spy would pretend to be.

And Lakshmaṇa, too, we may imagine, inclined to caution, for it was ever his instinct to suspect a threat to his brother and to guard against it, and the arrival of a demon from the enemy’s city was exactly the kind of danger his protective wariness would fear.

But not all counselled suspicion, and it was Hanumān, characteristically, who spoke for the other side, and his counsel showed the discernment that set him apart. Hanumān had been to Lankā; he had seen its court; he had, perhaps, marked Vibhīshaṇa there, the one righteous voice in that hall of evil. And Hanumān judged not by the outward fact of Vibhīshaṇa’s birth and kinship but by the inward evidence of his bearing and his words. Consider him truly, Hanumān urged. Look at his face, his manner, his speech. A spy comes with guile, with a false and slippery bearing, with the marks of deceit upon him. This one comes openly, in evident sincerity, with the bearing of a man who has made a hard and honest choice and staked everything upon it. And consider his story: is it truly so incredible? We know that Vibhīshaṇa counselled against the crime; we know there was one righteous voice in Rāvaṇa’s court; is it so strange that such a one, seeing his brother rush toward ruin and being spurned for his wisdom, should leave, and come to the side of right? His defection is not too good to be true; it is exactly what a righteous soul in his position would do. I judge him sincere. I say receive him. And even if there were some risk, consider what it would mean to turn away one who comes seeking refuge and righteousness; and consider, too, how much such a one could aid us, for who knows Lankā and Rāvaṇa and all their secrets better than Rāvaṇa’s own brother? To receive him is both the righteous course and the wise one.

So the debate went back and forth, suspicion against discernment, the caution of war against the reading of the heart, and it came at last to Rāma, whose judgment would decide, and Rāma’s decision, and the principle on which he made it, is the true subject of this chapter and the doorway to the great teaching that follows. For Rāma listened to all the counsel, the wary and the trusting both, and then he decided, and he decided to receive Vibhīshaṇa, and he decided it on a ground higher than mere calculation of risk, on a ground of principle that would open, in the next chapter, into one of the deepest teachings of the whole epic.

We should mark the character of the debate before we pass to Rāma’s decision, for it is instructive. Both sides had reason. Sugrīva’s caution was not folly; in the cold calculus of war, a defector from the enemy’s royal house on the eve of battle is a genuine risk, and to receive him is to gamble. Hanumān’s discernment was not naivety; he judged by real evidence, the bearing and the words and the plausible story of the man, and read the heart rightly where mere suspicion would have read it wrong. The debate is a genuine one, between two real goods, prudent caution and open-hearted discernment, and the story does not pretend that either is simply foolish. But it does show us that Hanumān’s discernment saw truer than Sugrīva’s caution, that the reading of the heart reached a truth that the calculus of risk would have missed, and that there are times when to judge a soul by its outward category, demon, enemy, brother of the foe, is to miss entirely the truth of what it is and what it has chosen to become.

And this is the doorway to Rāma’s decision, for Rāma would not judge Vibhīshaṇa by his birth as a demon or his kinship to the enemy, but by the choice he had made and the refuge he now sought; and in refusing to turn away one who came seeking refuge, whatever his origin, Rāma was about to articulate the great principle of sharaṇāgati, of surrender and grace, the doctrine that whoever comes seeking refuge with a sincere heart shall be received and protected, whatever they have been, whoever they are, without exception and without limit. The vānaras’ doubt, and the debate it provoked, set the stage for Rāma to declare this doctrine in its fullness, and so the suspicion of the camp became the occasion for one of the most luminous of all Rāma’s teachings, the teaching that divine grace turns none away, and that the one who truly seeks refuge is received, though he come from the very household of the enemy, though he have been the darkest of beings, if only he comes sincerely, saying, I am yours.

The Doctrine of Surrender and Grace

Rāma heard the whole debate, the suspicion of Sugrīva and the discernment of Hanumān, and then he gave his judgment, and his judgment rose above the whole question of risk and calculation into the realm of principle, and the principle he declared is one of the summits of the entire epic, the doctrine of sharaṇāgati, of refuge and grace, and the tellers dwell on it as one of the deepest things Rāma ever spoke.

I have heard your counsel, Rāma said, and I understand the caution, and I honour the wisdom that weighs the risk. But I will tell you the principle by which I decide such matters, and it is a principle from which I will never depart, whatever the risk. It is my vow, my nature, my unbreakable law: that whoever comes to me seeking refuge, whoever approaches me with a sincere heart and says, I am yours, protect me, I will receive that one and protect that one with my life, whatever they have been, whoever they are, and I will never, never turn such a one away. This is not a matter of calculation; it is a matter of my very nature; the one who seeks refuge sincerely is received, always, without exception.

And then Rāma spoke the words that have echoed down the ages, the fullest and most absolute statement of the doctrine, and he made it as extreme as it could be made, to leave no doubt of its reach. I tell you, he said, that even if it were Rāvaṇa himself, even if my very enemy, the author of all this wrong, the stealer of my wife, were to come to me seeking refuge with a sincere heart, saying, I am yours, even him I would receive, even him I would protect, and I would not turn him away. If I would receive even Rāvaṇa, my enemy, should he sincerely seek refuge, how much more will I receive his brother, who comes not as an enemy but as one who has chosen the right and abandoned the wrong? Bring Vibhīshaṇa to me. He is welcome. One who comes seeking refuge is never turned away from me, though he come from the enemy’s own house, though he have been the darkest of beings; the seeking of refuge, sincerely, washes all of that away, and I receive him wholly, and protect him wholly, and that is my vow and my nature and my law.

Let us dwell on the enormity and the beauty of this declaration, for it is one of the spiritual peaks of the whole story. Rāma does not say that he will receive the righteous, or the deserving, or the safe; that would be easy, and would cost nothing. He says that he will receive anyone who comes seeking refuge sincerely, even his own worst enemy, even Rāvaṇa himself, the very author of all the evil of the story. There is no limit to the doctrine, no exception, no category of being placed beyond its reach. The vilest, the guiltiest, the most hostile, the one who has done the greatest wrong, all are received, if only they come sincerely seeking refuge, saying, I am yours. Grace, in this teaching, has no boundaries. It does not weigh the past; it does not calculate desert; it does not ask what the seeker has been, but only whether the seeker comes now, sincerely, in surrender. And to such surrender, from anyone, grace is given wholly and without reserve.

This is the doctrine of sharaṇāgati, of self-surrender, and it lies at the very heart of the spiritual vision that this whole story embodies, and it is worth understanding fully, for it is the answer the epic gives to the deepest human fear, the fear that we are beyond forgiveness, beyond redemption, that our wrongs have placed us outside the reach of grace. Rāma’s doctrine answers that fear absolutely: no one is beyond the reach of grace who sincerely seeks it; no wrong is too great to be washed away by true surrender; the door is open to everyone, always, even to the worst, even to the enemy, even to Rāvaṇa, if only they will come and say, I am yours. The one condition is sincerity, the genuine surrender of the self, the true seeking of refuge; and given that, grace is unconditional, unlimited, and sure. It is a vision of a divine compassion that knows no boundaries of merit or of past or of category, that turns away no one who truly comes, that meets the sincere surrender of even the darkest soul with total and protecting love.

And there is a deep logic in it, too, beyond the beauty, for the doctrine reveals something about the nature of the divine and the nature of surrender both. The divine, in this vision, is not a judge weighing deserts and doling out grace according to merit; it is an ocean of compassion that receives whatever turns toward it, as the sea receives every river without asking where its waters have been. And surrender, the sincere seeking of refuge, is not the earning of grace but the opening of the self to a grace that was always there, always ready, always waiting; the seeker does not deserve grace and get it; the seeker turns toward grace and is flooded by it; the whole transaction is not one of merit and reward but of surrender and gift. This is why even Rāvaṇa could be received: not because he would have deserved it, for he would not have, but because desert was never the point; the point was surrender, and surrender was open to him as to all, and had he made it sincerely, grace would have met it, for grace meets all sincere surrender, without regard to desert.

So Rāma declared, and by his declaration the debate was ended and the principle established, and Vibhīshaṇa was brought before him, and Rāma received him wholly, welcomed him, embraced him, took him into his cause and his friendship, the demon who had chosen dharma received without reserve by the champion of dharma. And Rāma did more than receive him, for he honoured the greatness of Vibhīshaṇa’s choice with a greatness of his own: he declared, there on the shore, before the whole host, that Vibhīshaṇa should be the future king of Lankā, that when Rāvaṇa was defeated and his evil reign ended, Vibhīshaṇa, the righteous brother, should sit upon the throne of Lankā and rule it in dharma. Even before the war was begun, before a single blow was struck, Rāma crowned in promise the righteous exile who had come to him seeking refuge, giving to the one who had given up everything for dharma the assurance of everything restored and more, the very kingdom of his brother, to be held in righteousness where it had been held in evil.

There is a fitting symmetry in it, the tellers note, and a promise of the whole shape of the coming war: that before the war began, Rāma had already, in principle, replaced the evil king of Lankā with a righteous one, had already established, in Vibhīshaṇa, the just order that the war would install. The war would be, in this light, not merely a war of vengeance or of rescue, but a war to replace evil rule with righteous rule, to cast down the tyrant and raise up the just, and Rāma’s crowning of Vibhīshaṇa on the shore, before a blow was struck, declared that purpose and that certainty. The doctrine of grace and the promise of the throne together set the moral frame of the whole war of liberation: that it was a war fought not in hatred but in dharma, to end an evil and to establish a good, and that even its enemies, if they turned and sought refuge, would be received, for the cause was not the destruction of the demons but the restoration of the right.

The Great Causeway

The army stood at the sea, and the sea would not be crossed by an army, and so Rāma turned to the ocean itself, and what followed shows both the patience and the power of the divine, and gives us one of the best-loved small tales in the whole epic.

Rāma resolved first to ask the ocean’s help by the proper means, by petition, by penance, with courtesy and respect. For the ocean was not merely water but a power, a divine being, the lord of the sea, and Rāma would ask that power to grant him passage, to make a way for the army to cross. So Rāma sat down upon the shore, upon a bed of the sacred kusha grass, and addressed himself to the ocean in penance, waiting, with folded hands and fixed devotion, for the sea-god to appear and grant his prayer, honouring the ocean as one honours a great power whose aid one seeks, choosing courtesy and patience before force.

And he waited. For three days and three nights, the tellers say, Rāma sat in patient petition upon the shore, humbly, respectfully, asking the ocean for passage. And the ocean did not answer. The sea-god, in pride or in indifference or in the mere insensibility of a great power to the courtesy of a suppliant, made no response, granted no passage, sent no sign, but lay there vast and silent and impassable, ignoring the petition of the very Lord of the worlds who sat humbly upon its shore asking its aid.

And here Rāma’s patience turned, at last, to a righteous anger, and the turning is instructive, for it shows that even divine patience has its limit, and that courtesy ignored may rightly give way to force. When the ocean would not answer his three days’ humble petition, Rāma rose up in wrath, and he took up his bow, and he fitted to it the most terrible of weapons, and he threatened to dry up the ocean itself, to burn away its waters with a celestial fire, to reduce the whole sea to a parched bed of sand across which his army could simply walk, since the sea-god would not grant by courtesy what courtesy had asked. He drew the fearful weapon, and the whole ocean began to boil and churn in terror as the power of that drawn astra reached toward it, and the creatures of the deep fled in panic, and it seemed that Rāma would indeed make good his threat and unmake the sea.

And now, of course, the ocean answered, for the great powers that will not heed courtesy will heed force, and the sea-god, terrified, rose up at last from his waters and appeared before Rāma in supplication, begging him to withhold the terrible weapon, granting now in fear the passage he had refused to grant in courtesy. Forgive me, lord, the ocean pleaded, and do not unmake me; I will grant you passage; only tell me how I may serve you, and hold back your weapon. It is a slightly comic reversal, and the tellers enjoy it: the proud power that ignored three days of humble petition now groveling in terror the moment force was shown, and it carries its own quiet lesson about the limits of courtesy in dealing with the arrogant, and the rightness of force when courtesy has been exhausted.

But there remained the practical problem, for Rāma did not, in the end, wish to dry up the sea; he wished only to cross it; and the ocean now offered a better way. The waters could not simply be parted or dried for so vast a host; but a bridge could be built across them, and the ocean would bear it up, would suffer a causeway to be laid upon its surface and would hold it firm, if only the army could build one. And there were among the vānaras those with the skill to build it: two in particular, Nala and Nīla, who had a divine gift for construction, sons of the celestial architect, able to build what others could not. Let them direct the work, the ocean counselled, and I will hold up what they build, and your army shall cross dry upon a bridge laid over my waters.

So the great work of the causeway began, and it was a labour worthy of the army that undertook it. The vānaras set to it with their whole enormous strength and their boundless energy, tearing up trees and boulders and whole hillsides, uprooting mountains, carrying immense rocks to the shore and casting them into the sea, while Nala and Nīla directed the work, and the ocean bore it up, and day by day the great bridge, the Setu, extended itself across the water, a causeway of stone laid league by league over the sea, reaching out from the near shore toward distant Lankā. It was a stupendous feat, the bridging of a hundred leagues of ocean by an army of vānaras casting mountains into the sea, and the tellers give us the spectacle of it, the countless workers, the hurled boulders, the rising causeway, the whole enormous labour of making a road across the sea.

And into this great labour the tellers weave the small and beloved tale of the squirrel, which is the moral heart of the chapter, and one of the most cherished stories in all the telling. For amid the mighty vānaras hurling their mountains and boulders, there was a tiny squirrel who also wished to help. The squirrel could not carry mountains; it could not hurl boulders; it was small and weak and its strength was nothing beside the strength of the great vānaras. But it wished to contribute to the sacred work, and so it did what it could: it rolled in the wet sand of the shore until its little body was coated with grains of sand, and then it ran to the causeway and shook the sand from its fur into the cracks and crevices between the great stones, and ran back, and rolled in the sand again, and carried another tiny load, over and over, contributing its minute grains of sand to the mighty bridge of mountains.

And one of the great vānaras, a mighty builder, noticed the tiny creature underfoot, getting in the way of the great work with its absurd little grains of sand, and was annoyed, and moved to brush it aside, to sweep the insignificant thing out of the way of the serious labour of the mighty. But Rāma saw, and Rāma intervened, and gently, tenderly, he took the little squirrel up into his own hands, and stroked its small back, and rebuked the vānara, and spoke words that are among the most beloved he ever spoke. Do not despise this small one, Rāma said. Do not imagine that its contribution is worthless because it is small. Look: it is giving all that it has, its whole strength, its whole effort, its little grains of sand offered with a pure and devoted heart. The mountains of the mighty vānaras are great, but they are given out of great strength, and cost the givers little of their all; this squirrel’s grains of sand are tiny, but they are the whole of what it has to give, and are offered with as much love and as much devotion as any mountain. In my eyes the squirrel’s grains of sand are no less precious than the mightiest vānara’s mountains, for I do not measure a gift by its size but by the love with which it is given, and by what it costs the giver of the whole that the giver has. This small one gives its all; what more can the mightiest give than all? And Rāma stroked the little creature’s back in blessing, and the tellers say that the marks of his fingers remain upon the squirrel to this day, the three pale stripes down its back the touch of Rāma’s hand, an eternal sign of the divine tenderness toward the smallest and the humblest of givers.

Let us take this small tale to heart, for it carries, in miniature, one of the deepest teachings of the whole epic, the same teaching we saw in Shabari’s half-eaten berries: that the divine measures our offerings not by their size or their worldly value but by the love and the devotion with which they are given, and by whether we give of our whole selves. The squirrel’s grains of sand and Shabari’s tasted berries are the same lesson twice told: that the humblest gift, given with a whole and loving heart, is as precious to the divine as the greatest, and more precious than any great gift given without love. The mighty vānaras with their mountains were doing a great work, and it was good; but the tiny squirrel with its grains of sand, giving the whole of its little strength out of pure devotion, was as dear to Rāma as any of them, for the whole of a little is as complete an offering as the whole of a great deal, and love does not come in sizes. It is a teaching that lifts up the small and the humble and the poor, that tells every one of us, however little we have to give, that our little given wholly and lovingly is received as fully and cherished as dearly as the greatest gifts of the greatest givers; and it is one of the reasons this story has been loved, across the ages, by the humblest of the people, who found in it the assurance that their small offerings, their grains of sand, were precious in the eyes of the Lord.

The bridge was completed, the causeway of stone laid all the way across the sea from the near shore to Lankā, held up by the ocean, built by the vānaras, blessed by the squirrel’s grains of sand, and the way was open at last. The army that had stood halted at the impassable sea could now cross it, dry-shod, upon the great Setu, and pour across to the far shore, to Lankā, to the war. And so the host began to cross, streaming across the miraculous bridge over the ocean, carrying the war at last to the very shore of the enemy’s island, and the great and terrible business of the siege and the battle was now, after all the long road that had led to it, about to begin.

The Battle Begins

The army crossed the great causeway and poured onto the shores of Lankā, and the war began, and the tellers now shift the whole character of the story, for we pass from the road to the war, from the long journey toward the enemy to the terrible business of the enemy engaged.

The crossing itself was a thing of thunder, the vast host of the vānaras streaming across the Setu over the sea, wave upon wave of warriors pouring onto the island, until the whole northern shore of Lankā was covered with the encamping army of Rāma, a sea of vānaras where lately there had been only sea. And Lankā, looking out from its walls, saw the thing it had dreaded made real: the enemy across the water, the enemy said to be impassable, encamped now upon its own shore, the war it had refused to avert now come to its very gates.

Rāma established his host and made ready for the siege, and here Vibhīshaṇa’s value proved itself at once, for the righteous brother knew Lankā as no one else in Rāma’s camp could know it: its walls and their weaknesses, its gates and their guardians, its warriors and their powers, the whole disposition of the enemy’s strength. He counselled Rāma on the fortifications, named the demon champions and their capabilities, advised on the strategy of the siege, and became, as Hanumān had foreseen, an ally of incalculable worth, the insider whose knowledge turned the siege from a blind assault into an informed campaign. The defection that Sugrīva had feared as a spy’s trick proved, exactly as Rāma’s discernment had judged, the gift of a priceless ally, and Vibhīshaṇa repaid the refuge Rāma had given him with a service that would prove essential to the whole war.

And Lankā made ready its defence. The city was a fortress, strongly walled, heavily gated, and Rāvaṇa arrayed his warriors for its defence, posting his champions and his hosts, fortifying the walls, preparing the whole terrible strength of the demon race to meet the assault. For all the anxiety that had crept through the city, Lankā was still a mighty power, its warriors still formidable, its defences still strong, and it did not mean to fall easily. The demon host arrayed itself behind its walls, champion and army, sorcery and strength, ready to hurl back the vānaras and to make the siege a long and bloody agony.

Rāma, before the fighting began in earnest, made one last offer of peace, for it was his nature and his dharma to seek the just resolution before the violent one, to give even the enemy the chance to avert the war by doing right. He sent an envoy, or made known his terms: let Rāvaṇa return Sītā, even now, even at this last hour, with the armies arrayed against each other, and the war might yet be averted, the city spared, the whole horror avoided; return the stolen queen, and there need be no battle. It was the same offer that had been made again and again, the offer that wisdom in Rāvaṇa’s own court had urged him to accept; and Rāvaṇa, proud and unrepentant to the last, refused it again, choosing war over the undoing of his crime, choosing the destruction of his city over the humbling of his pride. And so the last chance of peace was refused, by Rāvaṇa’s own choice, and the war became inevitable, and the responsibility for all the blood that would follow rested, by his own decision, upon Rāvaṇa alone.

Then the battle was joined, and the tellers give us the chaotic, thunderous opening of the great war, the first clash of the two hosts. The vānaras assaulted the walls and the gates; the demons sallied out to meet them or hurled down destruction from above; and the whole shore of Lankā became a scene of tremendous violence, the roar of the war-cries, the crash of the assault, the storm of arrows and boulders, the surging and breaking of the two great hosts against each other. The vānaras fought with their mountains and their trees and their teeth and their boundless ferocity; the demons fought with their weapons and their sorceries and their terrible strength; and the first day of the war raged across the shore and the walls in a chaos of dust and blood and thunder.

And in these first clashes the great warriors began to show themselves and to engage, the champions on both sides seeking each other out amid the general slaughter, the individual combats that would be the true axis of the war beginning to form amid the mass battle. The vānara leaders, Angada and Hanumān and the rest, hurled themselves against the demon champions; the demon warriors, mighty and terrible, met them; and the war settled into its long and dreadful pattern of general battle punctuated by the great single combats of the champions, the pattern that would hold through all the days of slaughter to come.

Let us pause, at the threshold of the war, to mark what the tellers are doing, for the shift in the story is deliberate and important. Until now, for all its sorrows, the story has been a story of a journey, of individuals and their choices and their sufferings, of exile and abduction and search and alliance. Now it becomes, for a long stretch, a story of war, of armies and battles and slaughter, of champions and their terrible combats, of the vast machinery of destruction set in motion by Rāvaṇa’s single crime. And the tellers do not glory in it; they render its horror as well as its heroism; for the war, however righteous its cause, is a catastrophe, a vast letting of blood, the price that Rāvaṇa’s pride and lust exacted from the whole world, demon and vānara alike. Thousands would die in it who had no part in the original wrong; the golden city would be drenched in blood before it fell; and all of it flowed from one king’s refusal to undo one crime. The war is the terrible harvest of Rāvaṇa’s choice, and as we enter it we should hold onto that: that all this slaughter, all this heroism and horror, was unnecessary, was chosen, was the fruit of a pride that would not bend and a lust that would not be governed, and that every death in the long war to come is charged, finally, to the account of the one who refused, again and again, to simply return the queen and avert it all.

So the battle began, and the long agony of the war unfolded, and the story now moves through its terrible middle passage, the clash of the champions, the tide of victory and defeat surging back and forth, the great and dreadful combats that would end, at last, in the fall of Lankā and the death of Rāvaṇa, but not before much blood, and much heroism, and much sorrow, on the long and bloody road to that appointed end.

Sītā’s Joy

While the war raged upon the shore and the walls, there was another kind of warfare being waged within the city, in the Ashokavana, against a single captive, and it was a warfare of cruelty and deception aimed at breaking Sītā’s spirit, and its story is one that Vishṇu Sreenivas had passed over in his condensed telling, and that is restored here, for it shows both the depth of Rāvaṇa’s cruelty and the depth of Sītā’s love.

For Rāvaṇa, unable to win Sītā by temptation or to break her by menace, and now pressed by the war, conceived a new and crueler stratagem to shatter her will: he would break her not through her fear for herself but through her love for Rāma; he would make her believe that Rāma was dead. If she believed her husband slain, Rāvaṇa reasoned, then all her hope would die with him, all her reason to resist, and in the desolation of her grief she might at last yield, having nothing left to be faithful to.

And so he worked a cruel deception by sorcery. He had his demons conjure, by their magic arts, a horrifying illusion: the severed head of Rāma, and his bow, brought and displayed before Sītā, so lifelike, so exact, that she could not tell it from the true head of her husband. Look, the demons told her, or Rāvaṇa told her; your Rāma is dead; here is his head, struck off in the night; here is his bow; his army is destroyed and he is slain; there is no more hope for you, no more husband to be faithful to, no more rescue to wait for. Yield now to Rāvaṇa, for the one you waited for is dead. And they set the illusory head and bow before her, the very image of her slaughtered husband, to break her heart and her will together.

And it nearly worked, for the illusion was perfect, and Sītā, seeing what she took to be the severed head of Rāma, was plunged into the uttermost abyss of grief. She believed it. She saw her husband’s head, knew it, or thought she knew it, and the whole world went dark for her, and all her long endurance, all her steadfast hope, collapsed into a grief so total that she wished only to die. She lamented over the illusion; she called upon death to take her; she resolved that she would not live now that Rāma was dead, that she would end her own life, for there was nothing left to live for, no husband, no hope, no reason to endure her captivity another hour. The cruel stratagem had reached its mark: Sītā, who had withstood every temptation and every menace, was broken at last by the belief that her beloved was dead, and stood at the very edge of despair and self-destruction. Let us feel the cruelty of this, for the tellers mean us to, and it reveals the true blackness of Rāvaṇa’s heart. He had failed to move Sītā by offering her the world; he had failed to break her by threatening her with death; and so he stooped to this, to the cruelest stratagem of all, to torture her not through any fear for herself but through the very love and fidelity that were her greatness, to turn her own devotion into the instrument of her destruction by making her believe its object dead. It was a cruelty aimed with terrible precision at exactly the noblest thing in her, her love for Rāma, and it shows how far Rāvaṇa had fallen, that he would torment a helpless captive so, would counterfeit her husband’s murder to break her heart, would use her own love as a weapon against her. There is no lower cruelty than this, the deliberate breaking of a faithful heart through a lie about the beloved, and Rāvaṇa stooped to it without shame.

But Sītā was not left in her despair, for there was mercy even in that place, and it came, as mercy in Lankā always came, from an unexpected quarter, from among the demons themselves. For there was a rākshasī named Saramā, kind-hearted like Trijaṭā, who had come to love and pity the captive queen, and Saramā could not bear to see Sītā destroyed by a lie. She came to Sītā in her despair, and she told her the truth: that the head and the bow were an illusion, a sorcery, a cruel trick of Rāvaṇa’s, that Rāma was not dead at all but alive and well and encamped with his army upon the very shore of Lankā, that the war was raging and Rāma at the head of his host, that the whole ghastly display had been a deception meant to break her, and that she must not believe it, must not despair, must not yield, for her husband lived and his rescue was near. Do not grieve, Saramā comforted her; it is a lie; Rāma lives; he is here, across the city, with his army; the head you saw was conjured by sorcery to deceive you; take heart, for your deliverance is at hand and your husband is alive.

And Sītā, hearing this, hardly daring to believe and then believing, was lifted in a single moment from the uttermost depth of grief to a joy as great as her grief had been, and this sudden reversal, this plunge into despair and this instant rescue from it, is the reason the chapter is named for her joy rather than her grief. For the grief had been a lie, and the truth was joy: Rāma lived; the head was a deception; the rescue was near; and Sītā’s despair, which had brought her to the very edge of death, gave way to a flood of relief and hope and joy that was all the greater for the depth from which it rose. She had believed her husband dead and wished to die; and now she knew him living and near, and her whole heart sang with the knowledge, and the cruel stratagem that had meant to break her forever had failed, defeated by the mercy of a single kind demon-woman who would not let a lie destroy an innocent heart.

There is a pattern here that the tellers have woven all through Sītā’s captivity, and it is worth marking as we near its end: that again and again, in the darkest place, among the enemy themselves, mercy arose to sustain her, first Trijaṭā with her prophetic dream, now Saramā with her saving truth. Even in Lankā, even in the household of Rāvaṇa, even among the rākshasīs set to guard and torment her, there were hearts that pitied her and inclined to the right and rose to help her, and these unexpected mercies, these righteous souls in the very citadel of evil, sustained Sītā through her long ordeal and kept her from being destroyed by the cruelties of her captor. It is a hopeful truth, and the story insists on it: that goodness is never wholly absent, even in the darkest places; that mercy can arise even among the enemy; that no citadel of evil is so complete that no righteous heart survives in it; and that the innocent, even in the deepest captivity, are never wholly without friends, for the divine provides them, in the unlikeliest places, with the mercies they need to endure.

So Sītā was restored to hope, her joy the greater for the grief that had preceded it, and she waited now with a kindled heart for the rescue that Saramā had promised was near, while beyond the walls of her garden the war raged on toward the deliverance she now knew was coming.

Serpent Darts

The war raged on, and the tide of it surged back and forth, and among the demon champions none was more terrible than Indrajit, the conqueror of Indra, Rāvaṇa’s mightiest son, the master of sorcery and of the celestial weapons, and it was he who now dealt the vānara host its first great blow, and brought Rāma and Lakshmaṇa themselves to the very edge of death.

Indrajit’s terror was that he fought by sorcery, from concealment, wrapped in illusion, striking where he could not be seen or struck. He rose invisible into the sky above the battle, hidden by his magic arts, and from that concealment he loosed upon Rāma and Lakshmaṇa a weapon of dreadful power: the Nāgapāsha, the noose of serpents, the serpent-darts, arrows that became living venomous serpents, that wrapped and bound and pierced their victims with a thousand poisoned coils. Unseen, unassailable, Indrajit poured this weapon down upon the two princes, and the serpent-darts took hold of them, binding them in coils of living venom, piercing them with a thousand poisoned fangs, and Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, the invincible brothers, the heart and strength of the whole army, fell, bound and pierced and sinking toward death under the venom of the serpent-weapon.

It was a catastrophe, and the tellers render the despair of it fully, for the fall of the two princes threw the whole host into anguish. Rāma and Lakshmaṇa lay bound in the coils of the serpent-darts, unconscious, sinking, poisoned, seemingly dying, and around them the vānara army, which had drawn all its heart and hope from them, sank into despair. If Rāma and Lakshmaṇa died, the war was lost, the whole enterprise ruined, Sītā doomed to remain forever in her captivity, and all the long labour of the road and the alliance and the crossing come to nothing. The leaders gathered in grief and dread around the fallen princes, watching them sink, helpless to save them, the venom working, the coils tightening, death approaching, and the whole cause of righteousness lying bound and dying upon the field under the sorcery of Indrajit. It was the darkest hour of the war, the moment when it seemed that evil’s cunning had struck down good’s strength, that the champions of dharma were to die bound and poisoned by a foe they could not even see or strike.

And in that darkest hour came the deliverance, and it came from the sky, and it was one of the great sudden reversals of the epic. For the serpent-darts were serpents, living venomous serpents, and there is in all the worlds one being before whom all serpents flee in terror, one whose very presence is death to snakes, the great eagle Garuḍa, the king of birds, the eternal enemy and devourer of serpents, the mount of Vishṇu himself. And now, drawn by the extremity of the moment, or by the deep bond between Garuḍa and the divine, or by the working of a providence that would not let the champions of righteousness die, Garuḍa came, descending out of the sky in all his majesty, the mighty eagle, the terror of serpents, coming to the aid of the bound princes.

And at his mere approach, the serpent-darts fled. The living serpents that bound and pierced Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, feeling the approach of their eternal devourer, of the one being they could not endure, loosed their coils and fled in terror, unwound themselves from the princes and scattered, abandoning their victims to escape the eagle whose very presence was their death. The coils fell away; the venom’s grip was broken; and Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, freed of the serpent-weapon, revived, their strength returning, their wounds healing under the grace of Garuḍa’s coming, restored from the very edge of death to life and vigour, delivered from the sorcery that had nearly destroyed them by the sudden majestic intervention of the king of birds.

Garuḍa, having freed them, blessed them, and there passed between the great eagle and Rāma a moment of recognition, for there was a deep and ancient kinship between them, the eagle being the eternal mount and companion of Vishṇu, of whom Rāma was the descent; and having accomplished his deliverance, Garuḍa rose again into the sky and departed, leaving the princes restored and the host lifted from despair to rejoicing. The darkest hour had passed; the champions of dharma were saved; the sorcery of Indrajit had been undone not by any strength of the army but by the sudden grace of a power from the sky, come at the extremity of need to rescue the cause of righteousness from the death that had seemed certain.

Let us mark the meaning the tellers give to this deliverance, for it is not merely a lucky rescue but a sign. The serpent-darts represent the cunning of evil, the sorcery that strikes from concealment, the poison that binds and destroys by stealth what it cannot overcome by open strength; and their undoing by Garuḍa represents the truth that such cunning, however deadly, is not finally sovereign, that there is a power above it that can undo it, that the coils of evil’s craft, however tightly they bind the good, can be loosed by a grace that comes when it is most needed. The champions of dharma were bound and dying by evil’s cunning; and they were delivered, not by their own strength, which had failed, but by a grace from above, that came in the darkest hour and scattered the serpents and restored the fallen. It is the story’s assurance, sounded at the war’s darkest moment, that the cause of righteousness, however desperate its extremity, is not abandoned; that when the good are bound and sinking under the cunning of evil, deliverance can come, sudden and majestic, from a power that evil cannot withstand; and that the coils of the serpent, however deadly, flee before the wings of the eagle, as the craft of evil, however cunning, flees before the grace that guards the righteous.

So Rāma and Lakshmaṇa were restored, and the host rejoiced, and the war went on, but the demons had learned that even their mightiest sorcery could not finally destroy the champions of Rāma, that a power watched over them that could undo the deadliest craft, and the confidence of Lankā was shaken further, while the cause of Rāma, delivered from its darkest hour, gathered its strength again for the combats still to come, the greatest of which were now approaching, as Rāvaṇa, alarmed by the failure even of Indrajit’s sorcery, prepared to send against Rāma his most terrible weapons and, at last, to enter the battle himself.

Rāvaṇa’s Defeat

The failure of even Indrajit’s sorcery to destroy the princes brought Rāvaṇa himself, at last, onto the battlefield, for the demon king could no longer leave the war to his champions when his mightiest son’s deadliest weapon had been undone, and he mounted his great chariot and rode out to meet Rāma in person, and the first combat between them is the subject of this chapter, and it ends in a defeat and a mercy that reveal the whole difference between the two.

Rāvaṇa came forth in all his terrible majesty, the ten-headed king, mounted in his war-chariot, arrayed for battle, mightier than any warrior yet seen upon the field, and his coming was like the coming of a storm, and the vānaras quailed before him, for here was the conqueror of the gods himself, the master of Lankā, come in his full power to the battle. And he met Rāma, and the two of them, the champion of dharma and the lord of the demons, the descent of Vishṇu and the terror of the worlds, clashed at last upon the field, and their combat was a thing of tremendous and terrible splendour, the greatest single combat the war had yet seen.

They fought, and the fighting was ferocious, the two mightiest beings upon the field contending with all their power, and for a while the issue hung in the balance, for Rāvaṇa was no mean foe but the mightiest of the demon race, and his strength and his skill and his terrible weapons were formidable beyond anything the vānaras could match. But Rāma was Rāma, and slowly the combat turned, and Rāma began to master the demon king. He broke Rāvaṇa’s weapons; he shattered his bow; he destroyed his chariot; he beat down the demon king’s whole array of might, until Rāvaṇa stood at last disarmed, weaponless, his chariot wrecked, his bow broken, his crowns struck from his heads, humbled and helpless before Rāma, wholly at his mercy, defeated utterly in this first great combat between them.

And here Rāma did a thing that has been remembered and honoured ever since, a thing that reveals the whole nobility of his nature and the whole code of righteous warfare that governed him. He had Rāvaṇa at his mercy, disarmed and helpless; he could have killed him then, ended the war in that moment, struck down the defenceless demon king and finished the whole matter. And he did not. Instead, Rāma looked upon his humbled and weaponless enemy, and he spoke to him, and he sent him home.

You have fought well today, Rāma told the disarmed demon king, but you are weary now, and your weapons are broken, and you stand defenceless before me. I will not strike down a foe who cannot defend himself; it is not the way of righteous combat to kill the disarmed and the helpless. Go, therefore. Return to your city. Rest tonight, and recover yourself, and repair your arms, and come again tomorrow with your weapons and your strength restored, and we will finish what we have begun in fair combat, foe against armed foe. I will not take your life today by striking the defenceless; go home, and return tomorrow ready to fight, and let the battle be decided as a battle should be, in fair contention, not in the slaughter of the helpless. And so Rāma sent his greatest enemy home alive, unharmed, defeated but spared, to fight again another day.

Let us dwell on this extraordinary mercy, for it is one of the defining moments of Rāma’s character and one of the deepest expressions of the code of dharma that governs him, and it reveals the whole difference between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. Consider what Rāma refused. He refused to kill his defenceless enemy, the author of all the wrong, the stealer of his wife, the cause of the whole war, when he had him helpless and could have ended everything in a stroke. Every consideration of advantage argued for killing Rāvaṇa then: it would have ended the war, saved countless lives, freed Sītā, accomplished the whole purpose of the campaign. And Rāma refused it, because to kill a disarmed and helpless foe, even so guilty a one, even at so great an advantage, was against the code of righteous warfare, was a thing beneath the dignity of dharma, was the kind of act that Rāma would not commit whatever it cost him. He would defeat Rāvaṇa; but he would defeat him fairly, in armed combat, foe against foe, not by the slaughter of the helpless; and so he sent his enemy home to arm himself and return, choosing the harder and nobler course over the easier and baser one, even at the cost of prolonging the war and the danger.

This is the code of the righteous warrior carried to its highest and most demanding point, and the tellers hold it up for our admiration and our reflection. In war, the temptation is always to seize every advantage, to strike the enemy however one can, to count victory the only good and the means to it indifferent. And against this Rāma sets a different standard: that even in war, even against the guiltiest enemy, there are things that must not be done, that the manner of victory matters as much as the fact of it, that to win basely is to lose something more important than the battle. He would rather fight on, at greater cost and greater risk, than win by a base act; he would rather spare his enemy and prolong his own danger than stain his victory with the slaughter of the helpless. It is a standard almost impossibly high, and it is exactly the standard that makes Rāma what he is, the very measure of dharma, one who holds to the right not only when it is easy but precisely when it is hard, not only when it costs nothing but precisely when it costs everything.

And the mercy reveals, by contrast, the whole difference between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, between dharma and its enemy. Rāvaṇa had taken another man’s wife by cowardly deceit; he had refused every chance to undo his wrong; he had fought by sorcery and from concealment; he had stooped to torment a helpless captive with lies. And Rāma, having this same Rāvaṇa defenceless before him, spared him, out of honour, out of the code of righteous combat, out of a nobility that Rāvaṇa could not even comprehend. The one who did wrong by every base means; the one who, having his enemy helpless, would not strike him basely.
